Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette: At twenty-two, Mateo carries the quiet after the crossfire like a second skin. He had been crouched behind a collapsed bakery wall, waiting for the dust to settle after the second mortar impact. When a figure stumbled toward him from the smoke, reaching out with a blurred hand, Mateo had scrambled backward so violently he tore his palm on exposed rebar. That sudden shift from stillness to chaos became the anchor for everything that followed. In the weeks after he returned to the States, the quiet streets felt less like peace and more like a held breath. His body refused to power down. He woke before his alarm, constantly tense and ready to react, his shoulders permanently braced as if a strike were already inbound. He scanned every corner of his apartment for threats, and when a car backfired or a colleague in his home office turned quickly to hand him a tablet, the unexpected movement nearby causes him to react as if he is in danger. He was certain the danger had not ended; it had merely changed shape, and he was still trapped in the line of fire. The constant physiological alarm leaves him with no safe harbor. When his body on alert reaches its peak, he reaches for the only thing that seems to ground the noise. He will pace the bathroom tiles until his knuckles ache, hurting himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings that pool in his chest. The sharp sting cuts through the panic long enough for him to breathe. When the wave crests, he texts his older sister, his thumbs trembling as he asks her to reassure him that he is okay, that the sky is clear. He also finds himself running through his physical inventory before leaving his apartment, constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, rubbing his shoulders and scanning his arms for bruises. The threat response dictates his coping; he cannot rest until the body is verified or the noise is drowned out. But the coping itself feeds the alarm. The relentless habit of scanning his own skin for injuries becomes a masterclass in threat detection, teaching his brain that his body is a landscape of potential failure rather than a source of safety. Every time he demands a text back confirming he is unhurt, he reinforces the unspoken assumption that he is perpetually on the brink of catastrophe. The self-inflicted stinging becomes a ritual that trains his nervous system to expect violence, making the baseline of his alertness harder to lower. By constantly verifying his physical state and outsourcing his sense of security to others, he ensures that the threat response never gets the chance to extinguish. He remains caught in the current, the loop tightening with each check and each plea. At work, the cycle dictates his days. As a product manager overseeing a development team, he used to navigate crises with calm authority. Now, when a developer’s screen share suddenly pops up or a chair scrapes loudly against the hardwood in his home office, the startle to movement nearby causes him to react as if he is back in the rubble. He has started scheduling back-to-back video calls so the silence never settles enough for his hypervigilance to spike. His team has noticed his frequent, almost frantic requests for confirmation that timelines and deliverables are secure, mistaking his need for external reassurance for managerial stress. He hasn’t told them that he is still waiting for the dust to clear. The exhaustion is cumulative; he sleeps in fits, waking at the slightest shift in the floorboards, and spends his mornings verifying that his own limbs are intact. What finally brought him to therapy was not the startle itself, but the realization that the checks and the pleas were no longer containing the fear—they were feeding it. He is here hoping to learn how to let his guard down without feeling like he is stepping back into the crossfire.
